strengths: Introduces a much-needed benchmark for long-term RVOS, with videos averaging 60+ seconds vs. a few seconds in prior datasets, addressing a clear gap in the field.

Large-scale and diverse annotation effort: 2,193 videos, 6,703 objects, 163 object categories, 24,689 descriptions, built from multiple heterogeneous long-video sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), with a careful check-correct mask annotation pipeline using SAM2.

Thoughtful, explicit categorization of descriptions into static/dynamic/hybrid types enables fine-grained diagnostic evaluation of model capabilities, which is more informative than a single aggregate score.
Proposes two new metrics (tIoU, vIoU) that meaningfully extend evaluation beyond per-frame J&F to capture temporal presence/absence prediction, addressing a real limitation of existing benchmarks.
The oracle analysis with SAM2 given first-frame ground truth convincingly demonstrates that Long-RVOS poses substantially harder tracking challenges than MeViS, validating the benchmark's difficulty.

ReferMo is a reasonably well-motivated and simple baseline (keyframe + motion frame decomposition using MPEG-4 vectors, local-to-global architecture) that achieves consistent improvements over 6 SOTA baselines while maintaining competitive FPS, showing practical value as an efficient long-video baseline.

Comprehensive benchmarking of 6 SOTA RVOS methods trained under consistent settings provides useful comparative insights, e.g., revealing that SAM2-based methods may rely on tracking strength rather than language grounding, and models are biased toward static-type queries.
weaknesses: Mask annotation quality is not independently verified against manual ground truth; masks are generated by SAM2 propagation from sparse bounding boxes and human-corrected only when marked "inaccurate" by a small team, and there is no reported IoU/agreement statistic quantifying annotation accuracy or inter-annotator reliability, which is important given the reliance on automated tracking for a benchmark meant to evaluate segmentation precision.

The improvement of ReferMo over ReferDINO is relatively modest (48.7 to 51.3 overall J&F, and only 0.5% improvement on keyframes-only comparison in Table 3b), and ReferMo actually underperforms ReferDINO on tIoU, tempering the claimed "significant" gains for a paper whose core narrative is that motion-based local-to-global processing solves the long-video problem.

The paper does not clearly justify why MPEG-4 motion vectors (an engineering choice tied to specific compression parameters) generalize well or are preferable to standard optical flow beyond efficiency, and details on how motion vector-based keyframe segmentation interacts with variable/complex real shot changes are relegated to supplementary material, limiting reproducibility from the main text alone.

The tIoU and vIoU metrics, while useful, are relatively straightforward extensions of set-based IoU already used in related spatiotemporal grounding work (cited as inspiration), somewhat limiting the technical novelty of this contribution relative to its presentation as a major contribution.

Annotation process details raise potential concerns about scalability/cost and possible bias: only 20 college-student annotators and 3 expert validators / 9 correction annotators were used, and no explicit statistics on inter-annotator agreement or annotation guideline adherence are reported, making claims of "high-quality" descriptions and masks less rigorously supported.

The reliance on SAM2 for mask propagation both in dataset construction and in the ReferMo baseline (inference-time tracking) raises a potential circularity concern: since the ground truth itself was generated substantially by SAM2, and ReferMo also uses SAM2 for propagation, evaluating ReferMo's tIoU/vIoU that depend on SAM2 tracking quality may indirectly favor methods that also default to similar tracking behavior, which the paper does not discuss as a limitation.

The claim that current benchmarks lack temporal-consistency evaluation is reasonable, but the paper does not provide ablations isolating how much of the SOTA models' failure is due to language grounding versus tracking failure inherited from SAM2 errors, which would strengthen the diagnostic value of the benchmark.

strengths: Introduces the first large-scale, minute-level long-term RVOS benchmark (Long-RVOS), filling a clear gap since existing RVOS datasets (A2D-Sentences, JHMDB, Ref-DAVIS17, Refer-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) are limited to short clips of a few to tens of seconds; Long-RVOS averages 60.3s/video with 36.7 total hours, far exceeding prior datasets.

Careful, well-documented dataset construction pipeline: sourcing from TAO/VidOR/Ego-Exo4D for diversity and length, explicit selection criteria (duration, category filtering, multi-object with disappearance), a three-tier text annotation scheme (static/dynamic/hybrid) with a dedicated validation team, and an iterative check-correct mask annotation workflow using SAM2 plus manual correction.

Thoughtful new evaluation metrics (tIoU, vIoU) that explicitly capture temporal presence/absence consistency, addressing a genuine limitation of frame-averaged J&F metrics in the presence of occlusion/disappearance, which is well-motivated and clearly formalized.

Comprehensive benchmarking of 6 diverse SOTA RVOS methods (with and without SAM/SAM2) reveals an important and somewhat counterintuitive finding — that SAM2-based methods which excel on short-term benchmarks degrade substantially on long videos, suggesting overfitting to short-term tracking rather than genuine language-grounded reasoning, which is a valuable empirical contribution to the field.

The proposed ReferMo baseline is reasonably well-designed and computationally efficient (using MPEG-4 motion vectors instead of costly optical flow, and predicting masks only on keyframes with SAM2 propagation), and achieves consistent, non-trivial improvements across nearly all metrics and description types while maintaining competitive FPS.

Good supporting analyses: oracle analysis with GT-prompted SAM2 clearly demonstrates the increased inherent difficulty of long-term tracking in Long-RVOS versus MeViS, and ablations show the contribution of motion information and appropriate motion-length selection.
weaknesses: The mask annotation pipeline relies on SAM2 model outputs (bootstrapped from sparse boxes) refined by human correction rather than fully manual per-frame annotation; the paper doesn't report quantitative annotation quality metrics (e.g., IoU agreement with human-only annotation on a subset, or inter-annotator agreement), so the reliability of ground-truth masks at scale is not rigorously verified.

The text annotation process, while described with quality principles, lacks reported inter-annotator agreement statistics or measures of annotation consistency/ambiguity, especially important given the more open-ended and multi-type description scheme (static/dynamic/hybrid) compared to prior datasets.

The novelty of tIoU is somewhat incremental (essentially IoU on the temporal presence indicator), and while vIoU is a reasonable extension, the metrics are adapted rather directly from spatiotemporal video grounding works [40,52]; the manuscript does not analyze how these metrics correlate with or diverge from J&F in a nuanced way beyond the single observation that tIoU varies little across models.

ReferMo's improvement in tIoU is marginal or slightly worse than ReferDINO despite claims of the method addressing temporal consistency, which is only briefly explained (keyframe-only reasoning) without deeper investigation or a fix, leaving the trade-off partially unresolved.

The dataset is heavily skewed toward human instances (71.9%), which may limit its diversity claims regarding "163 object categories" being meaningfully balanced; the paper does not discuss how this skew might affect benchmark conclusions across object types.

Object masks on non-keyframes for ReferMo rely on a frozen pretrained SAM2 tracker rather than being learned/supervised, meaning ReferMo's reported performance is partly bounded by (and dependent on) an off-the-shelf model's tracking quality — this coupling could confound conclusions about the language-reasoning contribution versus tracking contribution, similar to the very criticism the paper levels at competing SAM2-based methods.

Limited comparison methods (6 baselines) and single-backbone (Swin-Tiny) evaluation restricts the generality of conclusions; no larger backbone or scaling experiments are shown to verify whether findings hold with more capable visual encoders.

The paper does not report annotation cost/time or discuss scalability of the human annotation pipeline (20 annotators, 3 experts, 9 correctors) for future dataset expansion, which is relevant for reproducibility and practical impact assessment.

strengths: Introduces the first large-scale, minute-level long-term RVOS benchmark (2,193 videos, avg 60.3s, 36.7h total, 2.1M masks), filling a clear gap relative to existing short-clip RVOS datasets (A2D-Sentences, Ref-DAVIS17, Refer-YouTube-VOS, MeViS).

Careful, principled dataset construction: sourcing from diverse long-video datasets (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), explicit selection criteria for occlusion/disappearance/multi-object videos, three distinct description types (Static/Dynamic/Hybrid) with clear annotation guidelines, and a rigorous check-correct SAM2-assisted mask annotation pipeline with expert validation.

Proposes two new, well-motivated metrics (tIoU, vIoU) that explicitly capture temporal presence/absence consistency, addressing a genuine blind spot of standard frame-averaged J&F metrics; empirical results show these metrics behave differently from J&F, supporting their added value.

Extensive benchmarking of 7 SOTA RVOS methods (both SAM/SAM2-based and non-SAM-based) reveals a clear and important finding: SAM2-based methods that excel on short-clip benchmarks degrade substantially in long-video settings, suggesting their gains stem from tracking rather than language-grounding, which is a useful diagnostic contribution to the field.

The proposed ReferMo baseline is reasonably well-designed (motion-vector-based clip decomposition, local-to-global architecture, keyframe-only supervision) and is efficient (comparable FPS to non-SAM baselines) while achieving consistent improvements across metrics and description types, plus favorable robustness to occlusion.

Thorough ablation studies (video decomposition, mask propagation strategies, global interaction, gating mechanisms, description length, event complexity, oracle SAM2 analysis) support the design choices and give good insight into what drives performance gains.

Supplementary material adds valuable attribute-level statistics (POC/FOC/OV/LRA/etc.) quantitatively demonstrating Long-RVOS is more challenging than MeViS, strengthening the claims of dataset novelty and difficulty.
weaknesses: Mask annotation relies heavily on SAM2 propagation from sparse box prompts with human correction; the actual per-object correction rate/error rate is not reported, leaving some uncertainty about ground-truth mask quality/consistency across a 2.1M-mask dataset, especially given SAM2's own oracle performance on Long-RVOS is only ~55-56% J&F, suggesting the automated pre-annotation itself may be imperfect on these long, difficult videos.

The dataset skews heavily toward human objects (71.9%), which may reduce claimed object diversity despite the large number of nominal categories (163), and could bias evaluation toward person-centric descriptions.

ReferMo's keyframe-only supervision with SAM2 propagation for non-keyframes means the method's temporal consistency metrics (tIoU/vIoU) are partly determined by SAM2's mask propagation behavior rather than purely by the language-grounding/global-interaction model, which somewhat entangles the contribution being evaluated and the tool being reused for annotation and inference alike (potential double-dipping/circularity concern given SAM2 is also used for GT mask generation).

The improvement of the proposed method, while consistent, is not dramatic in absolute terms (e.g., overall J&F 52.9 vs. 48.4 for ReferDINO), and the paper frames this as 'significant' rather more strongly than the magnitude might warrant for some readers; more statistical/significance analysis or variance across runs is not reported.

Details on annotator agreement/inter-annotator consistency for the text descriptions (beyond a 3-person expert validation team) are limited, and there's no quantitative measure of description quality/ambiguity resolution rate.

The dataset construction criteria (excluding fully static objects, requiring multiple objects with at least one intermittently visible) could introduce selection bias toward inherently challenging/occlusion-heavy videos, which, while intentional, means claims of ecological realism should be tempered as the benchmark is curated for difficulty rather than being a random long-video sample.

Comparison methods are trained only on Long-RVOS without external pretraining data (e.g., RefCOCO), which, while fair for benchmarking here, differs from how many of these methods are typically deployed/optimized in their original papers, potentially underestimating their true achievable performance and thus overstating the 'severe struggle' narrative.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: existing RVOS benchmarks are limited to short clips (a few seconds) with mostly salient objects, while Long-RVOS provides genuinely long (60+s), diverse videos with realistic challenges like occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, and shot changes.

Large-scale, carefully constructed benchmark: 2,193 videos, 6,703 objects, 163 object classes, 24,689 descriptions, with a rigorous multi-stage annotation pipeline (online platform, three annotator types, expert validation team, iterative check-correct mask refinement).

Thoughtful annotation design with three explicit description types (static, dynamic, hybrid), enabling fine-grained diagnostic evaluation of models' static-attribute vs. motion vs. spatiotemporal reasoning capabilities.

Introduction of tIoU and vIoU metrics is well-motivated and empirically shown to reveal information not captured by frame-averaged J&F (e.g., stable tIoU despite large J&F variance, uniformly low vIoU suggesting prior benchmarks overestimate robustness).

Extensive experimentation: 7 SOTA baselines evaluated, oracle analysis with SAM2 given ground-truth prompts (showing a striking ~25-point gap vs. MeViS oracle performance, quantifying task difficulty), and multiple insightful breakdowns (occlusion rate, description length, event complexity).

The proposed ReferMo baseline is reasonably well designed (motion-vector-based clip decomposition, local-to-global reasoning, gated image-motion fusion) and is supported by thorough ablations (video decomposition, mask propagation strategy, global interaction, gating mechanisms) demonstrating each component's contribution.

Dataset statistics (Table 8) comparing attribute frequencies (occlusion, reappearance, view/scale changes) against MeViS provide quantitative evidence that Long-RVOS is meaningfully more challenging, not just longer in duration.
Good practical consideration of efficiency (FPS reported), which is highly relevant for long-video processing and often neglected in RVOS papers.
weaknesses: Mask annotations are derived by first running SAM2 (an automated tracker) from sparse bounding-box prompts and then manually correcting errors; despite the check-correct loop, this pipeline could still propagate systematic tracking biases (e.g., in prolonged occlusions) that are harder to catch than fully manual annotation, and no quantitative mask-quality audit (e.g., IoU against a manually-annotated sample) is reported.
The dataset skews heavily toward human instances (71.9%), which somewhat undercuts the claimed 163-category diversity for the purposes of balanced object-class evaluation.

There is a slight tension in the paper's argument: it critiques SAM2-based competitors for having improvements that "primarily stem from SAM2's superior tracking" rather than language understanding, yet ReferMo itself also relies on SAM2 for all non-keyframe mask propagation, making the comparison to non-SAM2 baselines (SOC, MUTR, ReferDINO) somewhat asymmetric and the causal attribution of gains to the proposed architecture (vs. SAM2) less clean, even though ablations partially address this by isolating keyframe-only performance.

Text descriptions were collected from 20 college student annotators; no inter-annotator agreement or ambiguity analysis is reported for the three description-type categorization scheme, which could affect the reliability of the fine-grained Static/Dynamic/Hybrid evaluation splits.

ReferMo is described as a "simple" baseline, but the architecture (separate motion/image/text encoders, spatiotemporal attention, dual cross-attention, spatial/channel gating, global interaction with Hungarian matching) is fairly involved; the simplicity framing could be toned down or better justified relative to compute/parameter cost versus baselines.

The benchmark's underlying video sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) were not originally designed for RVOS, so scene/object diversity is inherited from and bounded by those sources' original collection biases, which is only partially mitigated by the curation criteria described.
Some presentation issues: the project page link is left blank, and dense tables (e.g., Table 3-6, 9-12) could benefit from clearer summarization or highlighting of key take-aways for readability.
